query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser cladding a Y and Hf co-doped protective coating onto bulk AlCoCrFeNi2.1 fasteners will improve their high-temperature oxidation, creep, and corrosion resistance by stabilizing the protective oxide layer and limiting microstructural degradation during extreme service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy fasteners with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
generation.intervention: Apply a laser-cladded, Y and Hf co-doped protective coating.
generation.conditions: Service conditions include extreme temperature fluctuations (e.g., prolonged exposure at around 900 °C in corrosive salt environments such as 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl), long-term mechanical loading, and room-temperature creep conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A doped surface layer enriched with yttrium and hafnium that forms a more thermally stable and adherent oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The Y and Hf dopants in the coating promote the formation of a stable and slow-growing protective oxide scale, which reduces hot corrosion spallation. This layer also mitigates surface defect formation and grain boundary diffusion under high-temperature and mechanically demanding conditions, thereby enhancing creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated fasteners will exhibit reduced oxide scale spallation, improved retention of high-temperature mechanical properties, and a lower creep rate compared to uncoated fasteners.
generation.baseline: The uncoated AlCoCrFeNi2.1 fasteners tend to show significant oxide scale spallation and performance degradation under high-temperature, corrosive, and prolonged mechanical loading conditions.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected under the specified high-temperature and corrosive environments, but the effectiveness of the coating may depend on optimized laser cladding parameters and precise Y/Hf doping levels; performance under different alloy compositions or drastically different operating conditions is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in oxidation resistance, creep rate, and mechanical property retention are uncertain and would depend on the coating thickness, uniformity, and dopant concentration achieved during laser cladding.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 fasteners: one set with the laser-cladded Y and Hf co-doped coating and one set uncoated as a control. Expose both sets to cyclic high-temperature conditions at 900 °C in a molten salt mixture (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) for 10 hours, followed by subjecting them to room-temperature creep and long-term mechanical loading tests. Post-exposure, analyze the surface for oxide scale spallation and the mechanical properties via standard tensile and creep tests.
measurements: Percentage area of oxide scale spallation (using SEM imaging)
Post-exposure hardness and yield strength (using nanoindentation and tensile tests)
Creep strain rates under standardized load conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated fasteners do not show statistically significant improvements in terms of reduced oxide scale spallation, enhanced retention of mechanical properties, and lower creep strain rates compared to the uncoated baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. Among the developed non-equiatomic HEAs, Co-rich TWIP and TRIP HEAs have superior room-temperature mechanical properties [,,], which were designed with the assistance of thermodynamic prediction, first-principle calculations, and experimental verification. The thermodynamic analysis reveals that the FCC-phase stability of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA decreases with the increase of the concentration of Co, and the FCC-phase is stable at a high temperature while the HCP-phase tends to be stable at ultra-low temperatures. Furthermore, the first-principle calculations demonstrated that an increase in the Co and Cr concentrations at the expense of Mn, Ni, and Fe could reduce the SFE and increase the elastic modulus and lattice friction stress of HEA [,]. It has been verified by experimental observations that a low SFE contributes to increasing the accumulation of dislocations by hindering their dynamic recovery, thus enhancing work hardening. Mechanical alloying is a potential synthesis technique for the production of flake-shaped HEAs with nanocrystalline structure [, ]. During the mechanical alloying process, the metal particles undergo repeated fracturing and cold welding with the synergistic effects of centrifugal force, hit force, squeeze force and friction force and are finally welded together. Alloying of metal particles at the atomic level is achieved through reduced diffusion distances, increased defect density, and heat released during ball milling. At the same time, under the action of various stresses, the metal particles produce severe plastic deformation and high density of dislocations. The annihilation and rearrangement of dislocations form subgrain boundaries. Nanocrystallines eventually form through grain boundary slip or grain rotation []. Therefore, the difference from other alloying techniques is that mechanical alloying has the advantages of achieving alloying at room temperature, excellent element solid solution ability, and element uniformity. reading.lever: Apply laser-cladded, Y and Hf co-doped protective coating on bulk AlCoCrFeNi2.1 fasteners to improve high-temperature oxidation, creep, and corrosion resistance.
reading.why: This intervention leverages demonstrated thermal stability and corrosion benefits from laser-cladded coatings on similar alloys to address the extreme environmental challenges of fastener applications.
